title: Adaptation to environment
summary: How organisms are adapted to the abiotic conditions of their habitats, how ranges of tolerance limit where species live, what conditions coral reefs need, and how temperature and rainfall shape the world's biomes.

keyterms.definition: The place where a community, species, population or organism lives, described by its geographical and physical location and type of ecosystem.
An inherited characteristic that makes an organism suited to its environment and way of life.
A non-living variable of the environment, e.g. temperature, water, light, soil pH, salinity and mineral nutrients.
The range of an abiotic variable within which a species can survive; it includes an optimum range and zones of physiological stress.
Part of the range of tolerance where organisms survive but with reduced growth and reproduction; beyond it is the zone of intolerance.
A line along which samples are taken at intervals to investigate how species distribution changes along an environmental gradient.
Grass adapted to dry, salty, shifting sand: rolled leaves, sunken stomata, hairs, thick cuticle and deep, extensive roots.
Tree of salty, waterlogged tidal swamps with aerial roots (pneumatophores) for oxygen, prop roots for support and salt excretion through leaves.
Reef-building corals need water under about 50 m deep, clear, 23–29 °C, salinity 32–42 ppt and pH above about 7.8.
Photosynthetic algae living mutualistically inside the tissues of reef-building corals.
A group of ecosystems with similar communities, resulting from similar abiotic conditions and convergent evolution.
Graph showing mean monthly temperature and rainfall at a location, used to compare climates of biomes.
Evolution of similar traits in unrelated species because they are adapted to similar environments.
Hot-desert species conserve water and lose heat (e.g. cactus spines, water-storing stems); rainforest plants have drip tips, buttress roots and climb for light.

questions.prompt: Which is the best definition of a habitat?
options: The role of a species in its ecosystem
All the organisms living in an area
The place in which a community, species, population or organism lives
The non-living factors in an ecosystem
questions.explanation: A habitat is where an organism lives, described by location and ecosystem type. The role of a species is its niche; all organisms in an area form a community.

questions.statement: A habitat can be described by its geographical location and by the type of ecosystem.
questions.explanation: For example, a habitat could be described as the sand dunes of a particular coast (location) and as a coastal dune ecosystem (type).

questions.prompt: Match each adaptation of sand dune grass (marram) to its benefit.

pairs.right: Trap humid air, reducing water loss
Reach water and anchor in shifting sand

questions.explanation: Sand dunes are dry, salty and windy, with sand that drains fast and moves; these adaptations conserve water and stabilize the plant.

questions.prompt: What is the function of the pneumatophores of mangrove trees?
options: To excrete salt from the roots
To obtain oxygen from the air for roots growing in waterlogged, oxygen-poor mud
To absorb water from the air during droughts
To store starch over winter
questions.explanation: Mangrove mud is waterlogged and anoxic, so roots cannot obtain enough oxygen from it. Pneumatophores grow upward above the mud and take in air through pores.

questions.text: Some mangrove trees excrete excess ___ through glands in their leaves.
questions.explanation: Mangroves live in seawater; removing salt prevents it reaching toxic concentrations in their tissues.

questions.statement: The adaptations of marram grass mainly help it to survive frequent flooding.
questions.explanation: Marram grass is adapted to drought, salt spray and burial by moving sand. Flooding tolerance is typical of mangroves.

questions.prompt: Which of these is an abiotic factor affecting the distribution of a plant species?
options: Soil pH
Competition with other plants
Grazing by herbivores
Infection by fungi
questions.explanation: Abiotic factors are non-living, e.g. soil pH, temperature, water, light, salinity and mineral nutrients. Competition, grazing and disease are biotic.

questions.text: A non-living variable such as temperature or salinity is called an ___ factor.
questions.explanation: Abiotic means non-living; biotic factors arise from other organisms.

questions.prompt: Why is each species found only in particular habitats?
options: Species choose habitats at random
All species can survive anywhere but prefer certain places
Organisms develop the adaptations they need after moving to a new habitat
Their adaptations suit them to a particular range of abiotic conditions
questions.explanation: Adaptations are inherited and evolve by natural selection over generations; a species thrives only where conditions fall within its tolerance. Individuals do not acquire adaptations because they need them.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes an adaptation?
options: A change an individual makes during its lifetime to cope with stress
Any behaviour learned from parents
An inherited characteristic that makes an organism suited to its environment
A response to an abiotic factor that lasts a few minutes
questions.explanation: Adaptations are heritable traits shaped by natural selection, not short-term responses or acquired changes.

questions.prompt: What is meant by a species' range of tolerance for an abiotic variable?
options: The value of the variable at which the population is largest
The range of values within which the species can survive
The distance over which the species is found
The time the species can survive without food
questions.explanation: The range of tolerance spans all values that allow survival, from one limit to the other; the optimum range lies within it.

questions.prompt: Put the zones in order along a gradient of increasing temperature.
questions.explanation: Population density is highest in the optimum range, falls in the stress zones on either side and is zero in the zones of intolerance.

questions.statement: Organisms in a zone of physiological stress can survive but show reduced growth or reproduction.
questions.explanation: Conditions are tolerable but not ideal, so fewer individuals are found there than in the optimum range.

questions.text: A line along which samples are taken at regular intervals to study changes in species distribution is a ___.
questions.explanation: Quadrats are placed at intervals along a transect while abiotic variables are measured at each point.

questions.prompt: A transect shows that a plant species becomes more abundant as soil moisture increases. What can be concluded?
options: Soil moisture causes the increase in abundance
The plant increases soil moisture
The plant cannot survive in dry soil
There is a correlation between soil moisture and abundance, but other factors could be responsible
questions.explanation: Field data show correlation, not causation; another variable that changes along the transect could be the cause. An experiment would be needed to test causation.

questions.prompt: Match each requirement for coral reef formation to its approximate value.
questions.explanation: These conditions allow enough light for zooxanthellae to photosynthesize and enough carbonate for corals to build their skeletons.

questions.statement: Reef-building corals need shallow, clear water because their zooxanthellae need light for photosynthesis.
questions.explanation: The algae supply the coral with sugars from photosynthesis, so reefs only form where light penetrates well.

questions.prompt: Why does a fall in ocean pH threaten coral reefs?
options: Less carbonate is available, so corals struggle to build calcium carbonate skeletons
Lower pH increases water clarity
Lower pH raises water temperature
Lower pH increases salinity above 42 ppt
questions.explanation: Dissolved CO2 lowers pH and reduces carbonate ion concentration, making it harder for corals to deposit calcium carbonate.

questions.text: Reef-building corals contain photosynthetic algae called ___ living in their tissues.
questions.explanation: This mutualism provides the coral with organic compounds; the algae gain shelter and nutrients. If stressed, corals expel them (bleaching).

questions.prompt: A plant species grows only where soil pH is between 5.5 and 7.0. What does this range represent?
options: Its niche
Its habitat
Its range of tolerance for soil pH
Its zone of intolerance
questions.explanation: The pH values within which the plant can survive are its range of tolerance for that variable; outside it lies the zone of intolerance.

options: A single ecosystem with one dominant species
All the organisms on Earth
The area where one population lives
A group of ecosystems with similar communities due to similar abiotic conditions
questions.explanation: Biomes such as tropical rainforest or hot desert occur on several continents wherever the climate is similar, and they share similar types of community.

questions.text: A graph showing mean monthly temperature and rainfall at a location is called a ___.
questions.explanation: Climographs let you compare the climates of different biomes and explain their distribution.

questions.statement: Temperature and rainfall are the main abiotic factors determining the distribution of terrestrial biomes.
questions.explanation: Combinations of these two variables largely determine which biome develops, e.g. hot and wet gives tropical rainforest; hot and dry gives desert.

questions.prompt: Match each biome to its climate.

pairs.right: Very low rainfall, high daytime temperatures
Moderate rainfall with warm summers and cold winters

questions.explanation: Each biome's community reflects its temperature and rainfall pattern, as shown on climographs.

questions.prompt: American cacti and African euphorbias are unrelated but both have fleshy, spiny, water-storing stems. This is an example of:
options: Divergent evolution
Convergent evolution
Adaptive radiation from a common ancestor
Acclimatization
questions.explanation: Similar selection pressures in hot deserts have produced similar traits in unrelated lineages, which is convergent evolution and explains why biomes have similar communities.

questions.statement: Organisms in the same biome on different continents are always closely related.
questions.explanation: They often look alike because of convergent evolution, but they may belong to quite different lineages.

questions.prompt: Which is an adaptation of cacti to life in hot deserts?
options: Large, thin leaves for maximum light absorption
Drip tips to shed heavy rain
Leaves reduced to spines and swollen stems that store water
Buttress roots for support in shallow soil
questions.explanation: Spines greatly reduce the surface for water loss and deter herbivores, while the green stem photosynthesizes and stores water.

questions.prompt: Which is an adaptation of plants to tropical rainforest conditions?
options: Thick cuticle and sunken stomata to conserve water
Swollen stems that store water
Deep taproots to reach groundwater
Leaves with drip tips that shed heavy rain quickly
questions.explanation: High rainfall means water must run off leaves quickly, reducing growth of fungi and algae. The other options are water-conservation adaptations typical of deserts.

questions.text: The fennec fox of hot deserts has very large ___ that help it lose heat.
questions.explanation: Large, thin ears with many blood vessels give a big surface for radiating heat, and they also help locate prey.

questions.prompt: Many tall rainforest trees have buttress roots. What is their main advantage?
options: They store water for the dry season
They support tall trees growing in shallow soils
They take in oxygen from waterlogged mud
They excrete salt
questions.explanation: Rainforest soils are often thin, so roots spread near the surface; buttresses widen the base and stabilize tall trunks.
